claims.text: The starting coating is an as-deposited dual-phase material containing FCC regions and embedded BCC precipitates or interphase regions.
The starting coating has a moderate FCC/BCC interphase-boundary density.
Changing thermal gradients or applying a controlled post-deposition treatment can increase FCC/BCC boundary density.
Such processing can increase FCC/BCC interface coherence.
FCC/BCC boundary density and coherence can be increased without changing the overall phase fractions.
A higher density of FCC/BCC interphase boundaries impedes dislocation glide.
Greater FCC/BCC interface coherence makes the interfaces more effective barriers to dislocation motion.
The interphase boundaries disrupt continuous dislocation glide by causing dislocations to bow or pile up.
Dislocations may be annihilated at FCC/BCC interfaces during creep.
Impeded dislocation motion at FCC/BCC interfaces reduces the creep strain rate under sustained loading.
A coating with a higher density of coherent FCC/BCC interfaces will have a significantly lower creep strain rate than the as-deposited baseline.
The proposed interface effect operates in temperature and stress ranges where creep is predominantly controlled by dislocation motion.
At very low temperatures or extreme stresses, other deformation mechanisms may diminish the influence of FCC/BCC interphase boundaries.
FCC/BCC interphase boundaries, deformation twinning, and fine BCC/B2 precipitates jointly contribute to exceptional work hardening in a dual-phase FeCoCrNiAl0.5 alloy.
Al addition can transform CoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloys from FCC toward BCC structures and can improve nanoscale creep resistance, with a nonmonotonic dependence on Al content.

Failure to observe both a statistically significant creep-rate reduction and dislocation impediment at interfaces in the engineered samples would falsify the proposed governing role of the interfaces.
